svg.text: Raw edge-energy panels still matter, but near-lock slope is the honest quantity when the question is normalized loop gain.
One fix to the previous band-edge panel: raw imbalance is not the same thing as calibrated near-lock gain

text.tspan: The first sidecar got the branch choice right: band-edge logic really does need excess bandwidth. This follow-up checks the narrower question that was still open — whether the height of the
raw edge-energy panel should also be read as the actual FLL discriminant gain.
At Δf / R_s = 0.10 and 255 taps, the bounded
edge-energy imbalance grows from 0.019 at α = 0.05 to

svg.text: But the slope story is tighter

text.tspan: With the same 255-tap filters, the near-zero slope
only moves from 0.958 at α = 0.20 to 1.006 at α =
0.50. That is much less alpha-sensitive than the raw
imbalance height.
At α = 0.05 the slope stays soft even with longer
filters. That looks like both a waveform problem —
little excess bandwidth — and a filter-design problem,
not just a vague lack-of-energy slogan.

svg.text: 1. The raw edge-energy cue still rises hard with roll-off

text.tspan: This is the same bounded imbalance used in the earlier sidecar: upper edge energy minus lower
edge energy, divided by total signal energy. It is a good intuition panel for whether excess
bandwidth leaves a visible clue at all.
At 255 taps, α = 0.50 shows about 4.7× the raw imbalance
of α = 0.05. That is exactly why the earlier intuition
panel still belongs in the repo.

svg.text: 2. Near lock, the normalized slope tells a tighter story

text.tspan: This panel switches to a central finite difference around zero CFO. The y-value is d(error) /
d(Δf / R_s), so an idealized normalized slope of about 1 becomes the practical reference line
instead of the raw imbalance height.
At 255 taps the slopes are 0.958, 0.983, and 1.006 for α =
0.20, 0.35, and 0.50. That is much flatter than the raw
imbalance panel.
α = 0.05 only climbs to
0.508, which is why the
tiny-roll-off case still
looks genuinely fragile.

svg.text: 3. The honest read: keep the old intuition panel, but stop treating it like a loop-gain calibration plot

text.tspan: This follow-up does not retract the earlier waveform-domain comparison. It just makes the calibration claim precise enough to trust. The raw panel still answers whether excess bandwidth leaves a
usable clue. The slope panel answers how close the near-lock discriminator is to its normalized target once the filters are long enough.
Band-edge logic belongs in the excess-bandwidth
branch, not in the PSK-symmetry branch.
A raw imbalance panel is still the clearest first
intuition for that difference.
Rename that panel as raw imbalance so readers do
not mistake it for calibrated gain.
Use the near-zero finite-difference slope when the
question is loop sensitivity, not just visual clue
strength.
Swap in a band-edge design closer to the GNU Radio
/ fred harris construction and compare the slope
again.
Keep the same 4 sps setup so the repo stays about
one clean distinction instead of sprawling into a
modem survey.
Bottom line: the old sidecar got the branch choice right, but this one closes the loophole. Raw band-edge imbalance gets much bigger with roll-off; the normalized near-lock slope gets far
less alpha-sensitive once the filters are long enough. Those are related facts, not the same fact.
